title: What Slash Commands Actually Do
body_markdown:
Somebody at Gusto asked, during one of our internal AI AMAs, whether /login was costing them tokens. The answer came back yes, relayed into our Claude Code channel a few minutes later: /login "is an LLM call, which will take more time and end up with unnecessary token use," so run claude auth login from the CLI instead, because that one's instant and free. It came with receipts, sort of. Secondhand from someone who'd watched /login run up $3.


That felt off, so I went and checked. It’s off. /login never touches the model, in any config. It's a local command: it runs entirely on your machine and never builds a prompt, so there is nothing to send.


So where did the $3 come from? A leading space. /login with a space in front doesn't run as a command; it goes to the model as plain text, which really can cost you money. That same bug had already turned up that same hour, in the same channel, on a different slash command. I only made the connection to /login while chasing down the claim.


Gusto, like most of the industry right now, is pushing engineers to use LLM tools and share what they learn with each other. Everybody is learning in public, in channels and DMs and blog posts, and fast. Tips get passed along. Some are right. Some were right the last time somebody checked. And when the tip is about what something costs, reading it won’t tell you which kind you got.


Slash commands all look the same when you type them. Four different mechanisms sit behind that one leading /, and which one you got determines whether you paid for tokens, whether your hooks fired, and whether the thing you typed even ran. Worth knowing which one you're getting.


### 1. The Four Kinds


The split that matters is the one Claude Code itself uses. Its categories decide whether you get billed and whether a hook fires, so they’re the ones that predict behavior, even where they cut across the categories in your head.


[Mods](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview) , Claude Code’s JavaScript plugin API, are the clearest place to see this. Their[TypeScript declarations](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/main/mods/types/claude-code.d.ts) (which Anthropic’s docs call the complete reference) describe a command’s output as “a local command's returned text," so that's the name this post uses for commands that run on your machine and stop there.


From the outside, a slash command is one of four things:


1. A **literal prompt** that ships with Claude Code. Typing it is the same as typing that text yourself. /init, /team-onboarding.
2. A **bundled skill** , a skill that ships inside Claude Code and builds its prompt when you run it. /debug, /doctor, /loop, /schedule, and more.
3. A **local command** , which runs client-side code and never builds a prompt. It might pop a UI, change some state, print something. /login, /clear, /model, /context, /help, and most of the rest.
4. **Something you or a plugin wrote** , a markdown file on disk that becomes a prompt. Every skill you’ve ever written is here, as is anything under .claude/commands/.


You can watch Claude Code tell the first two apart. The UserPromptExpansion hook's command_source field reads builtin for /init and bundled for /debug.


Only 1, 2, and 4 build a prompt. Category 3 is most of the built-in list, which is why most slash commands you type are free (mostly; see the next section).


The vocabulary has been moving, so it’s worth one paragraph. Anthropic used to call category 4 “custom commands,” now treats .claude/commands/*.md as legacy, and steers new work to skills/*/SKILL.md. So depending on when a doc was written, the same file on disk is a command or a skill, while categories 1 through 3 are also all called commands. The mechanism is stable even though the names are still settling.


One thing that trips people up: a user-invocable skill *is* a slash command, specifically the fourth kind. Typed, a skill fires the same hooks /init does. Claude reaching for the same skill on its own produces the same transcript record, so it looks like the only difference is who pulled the trigger. That turns out to matter a lot if you ever try to measure this.


### 2. Which Ones Cost Tokens


The handful of built-ins that cost you a completion are the literal prompts (/init, /team-onboarding) and the bundled skills, /debug and /doctor and /loop among them. /insights is the outlier: it's registered as a literal prompt, but when I ran it, it kicked off its own analysis on a bigger model and cost me more than a dollar. Everything else built in is local: /login, /clear, /model, /compact, /status, /context, /help, /resume, and a long tail after that. The exact list moves every release, so I'm not going to pretend a count would stay true.


Anything you or a plugin wrote is presumptively a prompt. A markdown file under .claude/commands/ or a skill's SKILL.md becomes a message to the model, which is mechanically the same thing a baked-in prompt command does, just loaded from disk. So "is this slash command free" only has a knowable answer for the native ones.


This means every skill costs tokens, both the body of the SKILL.md and whatever Claude does with it, whether you typed it or Claude reached for it.


Local doesn’t always mean free, though. A few local commands make their own side calls: /compact summarizes your conversation, and /rename with no argument has the model come up with a name. And some cost happens with no command at all. Claude Code ships an optional built-in mod,[you-should-know](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview#mods-built-into-claude-code) , that runs a side agent alongside longer tasks and pops up notes when it spots something you might miss. That's model usage you never typed. /login is still free, though.


And it puts the original claim to rest. /login is in the free bucket, and claude auth login does the same sign-in from outside a session. Neither one is cheaper, because neither one costs anything.


#### Mechanisms, and How We Know


Everything above you can see from the outside. The rest gets into mechanism, so it’s worth being explicit about where each claim comes from.


Most of it comes from Anthropic’s public docs, mainly the[hooks reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) , the[monitoring and telemetry page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage) , and the newer[mods docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview) , which ship a TypeScript declarations file that spells out every event, payload, and tool schema in the harness. The rest comes from running hooks against a real session and looking at what showed up. Where a claim rests on a run instead of a doc, I say so.


I dug into this in two passes. By the time the post was ready, Anthropic had published docs covering much of what I’d been piecing together, so I re-ran the hook tests and swapped the docs in as sources.


### 3. The Four Invocation Paths


```text
+------------------+---------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |       Path       |                     Prompt built by                     |                                      What hooks see                                      |  +------------------+---------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  | Literal prompt   | text that ships with Claude Code                        | UserPromptExpansion plus UserPromptSubmit (command_source: builtin)                      |  | Bundled skill    | the skill, at invocation                                | UserPromptExpansion (command_source: bundled) plus UserPromptSubmit                      |  | Local command    | never                                                   | no classic hook; a mod's command.run (see below)                                         |  | On-disk markdown | the file, plus any inline shell commands, at invocation | UserPromptExpansion (command_source: projectSettings, plugin, ...) plus UserPromptSubmit |  +------------------+---------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```


That fourth row is skills and .claude/commands/*.md, the stuff you and your plugins wrote. It's the path everybody already knows about, since it's how you author anything.


Less known: a SKILL.md body supports an inline shell substitution.


```text
!`some-command $ARGUMENTS`
```


That command runs at invocation and its stdout gets spliced into the prompt before the model sees anything. It’s a real capability, and people ship real tools on it. Anthropic also ships an off-switch for it:[disableSkillShellExecution](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#disableskillshellexecution) in settings, which replaces those commands with a placeholder instead of running them. A shell:[frontmatter key](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills) picks bash or powershell, defaulting to bash on every platform.


One thing the table hides: the three prompt-building paths end up in the same place. The mods API has a single skill.prompt event, documented as firing whether a skill was "typed as /name, called through the Skill tool, or preloaded into a subagent: the same event at each." Everything that tells them apart happens before that point. (One catch if you try to hook it: in my runs, where Claude Code's built-in security mod loads, as it does under managed settings, it handled skill.prompt first and passed it on past the mod I'd installed, so mine never saw it.)


There’s also a whole layer in front of all this, deciding how many commands one line of input turns into. That’s a separate post.


### 4. Hooks Can’t See Local Commands (But Mods Can)


This falls straight out of the four-way split. If a command never builds a prompt, none of the hooks in your settings.json fire for it. UserPromptSubmit and UserPromptExpansion both hang off the prompt pipeline, and a local command never enters it.


I tested this: /clear, /context, /model, and /compact fire neither, despite visibly doing something on your screen. So if you've written a hook to catch someone running /clear and it never triggered, that's why, and no matcher on a prompt event will fix it.


Classic hooks can still catch the *effect* . SessionStart takes clear and compact as matcher values, and compaction gets PreCompact and PostCompact with manual or auto, so you can tell a typed /compact from an automatic one.


Mods change this. A mod is a plugin with a JavaScript hooks module instead of shell commands, and one of its events is[command.run](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/reference) , which fires for every slash command you type. I checked /clear, /context, /model, /compact, /debug, /init, and a plugin skill, and it fired for all of them. Claude Code's own bundled diff mod[hooks](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/e47cc82bdbd27b5f799acd5b05fd0c29d33bb48c/mods/diff/hooks/register.ts#L899)[/clear and](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/e47cc82bdbd27b5f799acd5b05fd0c29d33bb48c/mods/diff/hooks/register.ts#L899)[/resume](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/e47cc82bdbd27b5f799acd5b05fd0c29d33bb48c/mods/diff/hooks/register.ts#L899) this way, to reset its pane. A mod can also answer command.run itself without calling through, in which case the command never runs.


So the rule is that the prompt hooks only see commands that build a prompt, and a mod sees every command you type. Neither one sees a skill Claude reaches for on its own, which is the next section.


### 5. Skills Have Two Entry Points


Type a skill and it goes down the same path as /init: the same hooks fire, and it lands in the transcript the same way. There's no separate skill pipeline for the typed door.


What differs is how you get in, and there are two doors:


```text
+--------------------------+---------------+---------------------------------------+  |       What differs       | You type /foo | Claude invokes foo via the Skill tool |  +--------------------------+---------------+---------------------------------------+  | UserPromptExpansion      | fires         | does not fire                         |  | UserPromptSubmit         | fires         | fires                                 |  | PreToolUse / PostToolUse | no            | yes, tool_name: "Skill"               |  | Transcript record        | yes           | yes, and it looks the same            |  +--------------------------+---------------+---------------------------------------+
```


Anthropic’s own docs confirm both doors. Per the[skills docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills) , disable-model-invocation: true is for *"workflows you want to trigger manually with* */name,"* and with user-invocable: false, *"Claude Code hides it from the* */ menu and doesn't run it when you type* */name."* The mods API goes further and names a third door: its skill.prompt event is documented as firing for a skill "typed as /name, called through the Skill tool, or preloaded into a subagent." Those settle who can come in through each door. Which hooks fire at each one is what I went and measured.


**The row that matters is** **UserPromptExpansion.** It fires only when a person types the command. The Skill tool skips it entirely. So UserPromptExpansion sees human-typed skills and is blind to model-invoked ones, and PreToolUse on Skill is blind in exactly the opposite direction.


That asymmetry matters because both entry points produce transcript records that look alike, so every obvious approach to measuring skill usage picks one door and misses the other.


One smaller thing while we’re here: a skill can register its own[hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills) when it loads, including[one-shot hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#hooks-in-skills-and-agents) that remove themselves after firing. So a skill can install a Stop hook without ever touching your settings file.


**How much of this is measured.** All of it, in both directions. I typed a plugin skill as /name, then asked Claude to invoke the same skill through the Skill tool, with logging hooks on everything. Typed: UserPromptExpansion fired, PostToolUse on Skill didn't. Model-invoked: the reverse. A mod's command.run lined up with the typed door too, firing for /name and staying silent when Claude invoked it.


I also hit this by accident before I went looking: a plugin’s telemetry never fired for a human-typed skill, because typing a skill doesn’t create a Skill tool call at all. A skill invoked from inside another skill does produce a normal Skill tool call. The one case I haven't exercised is a skill invoked inside a forked subagent.


### 6. The skill_activated Telemetry Event


There’s a third surface that sees both doors at once, which makes it the most attractive option on paper, with one catch in practice.


Claude Code emits a[skill_activated](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage#skill-activated-event) telemetry event from both entry points, carrying an invocation_trigger field: user-slash when a human typed it, claude-proactive when the model reached for it, and nested-skill for a skill fired from inside another one. Alongside skill.source, skill.kind, plugin.name, and marketplace.name (the last two only appear with OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 or for official-marketplace plugins). That's richer attribution than either hook gives you, and it costs no code at all.


The catch is name redaction. Per the[monitoring docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage) , skill names from user-defined skills and third-party plugins show up as the placeholder custom_skill unless OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 is set. Built-in and bundled skills come through by name.


That’s a sensible privacy default, since a skill’s name can say a lot about what you’re working on. Skills we author at Gusto ship in our own plugins, so they redact. The gate is an environment variable on the machine running Claude Code, not something a plugin controls, so flipping it fleetwide is an infrastructure conversation rather than a code change.


The cost metrics carry a skill.name attribute too, and its description is a nice independent confirmation of the two-entry-points premise. Anthropic describes it as *"set by the Skill tool or a* */ command, or inherited by a spawned subagent."* Three entry points, named explicitly, in their own docs.


One trap: that attribute’s redaction rules are different from skill_activated's. There, user-defined skill names appear verbatim and only third-party plugin skills get redacted. Check which signal you're reading before you trust a name.


### 7. Counting Skills Properly


This is the actionable one.


Counting skill usage accurately is harder than it looks, and the reason is structural rather than anyone’s bug. The obvious approach, and the one that was available before anyone noticed these hooks, is to scan transcripts when the session stops: regex for <command-message> tags, separately look for Skill tool_use blocks, emit both as identical records.


That’s a reasonable design given what used to be visible. It has three problems, and all three are consequences of transcript scraping being the only visible surface.


**A good chunk of what it reports as skill usage isn’t skills at all.** Measured against my own skill-usage log, roughly one event in six is a native client-side command. /clear dominates, and it would rank near the top of a most-used-skills dashboard despite never involving a skill. /model, /plugin, /mcp, /login are all in there too.


The polluting set also drifts in both directions. /model started showing up in my log right after I'd written a note saying it leaves no transcript trace. /exit shows up on one day in May and never again. So a static exclusion list can't hold, and the metric drifts every time Claude Code adds or changes a command.


The two detectors are also indistinguishable downstream, because both emit the same record shape, and later processing overwrites the one field that separated them.


**They also overlap, so some invocations get counted twice.** The two-entry-points section explains why: a model-invoked skill produces a Skill tool_use block *and* a <command-message> transcript record. Both detectors fire on one invocation. The log agrees, with a few dozen record pairs sharing a session, a skill name, and an identical millisecond timestamp. Most of them are skills Claude invoked on its own because an instruction file told it to, which is what you'd expect if one invocation writes both records. It's a few percent of inflation on top of the pollution, and it lands hardest on the skills a dashboard would call most-used.


#### What to Do Instead


The hook event is UserPromptExpansion. It's on the[public hooks page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) , described as firing "when a user-typed command expands into a prompt, before it reaches Claude," with a matcher documented as matching on command name. The payload shape is spelled out in the mods[TypeScript declarations](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/main/mods/types/claude-code.d.ts) , which carry the full input type for every classic hook too:


```text
type UserPromptExpansionHookInput = BaseHookInput & {    hook_event_name: 'UserPromptExpansion';    expansion_type: 'slash_command' | 'mcp_prompt';    command_name: string;    command_args: string;    command_source?: string;    prompt: string;  };
```


Local commands never reach it, so the pollution can’t happen. You get command_name directly, and command_source separates bundled builtins from things loaded off disk, which transcript scraping can't do at all.


It isn’t enough on its own, though. It fires on the typed path only, so adopting it as your single source trades an overcount for a silent undercount of every model-invoked skill.


**Use two hooks and the coverage closes.** The Skill tool is an ordinary tool, so PostToolUse with matcher: "Skill" catches everything UserPromptExpansion misses, and the two don't overlap. I checked: a typed skill fires only the first, and a model-invoked one fires only the second.


```text
+---------------------+------------------+-----------------------+-------------------+  |        Hook         |     Matcher      |        Catches        | Where the name is |  +---------------------+------------------+-----------------------+-------------------+  | UserPromptExpansion | the command name | a human typed /foo    | command_name      |  | PostToolUse         | Skill            | the model invoked foo | tool_input.skill  |  +---------------------+------------------+-----------------------+-------------------+
```


Neither one needs parsing. The Skill tool’s input, in the same declarations file, is { skill, args }, so the name is a field lookup. The transcript scanning, the watermark file, and the regex all go away, and which hook fired tells you which entry point it was.


One limit, measured the hard way. The Skill tool’s *output* , per the same file, carries commandName plus a status of inline or forked, but a PostToolUse hook on Skill doesn't get to see it. Live testing showed the hook payload carries only {success, commandName}, with no tool output at all. So you can count invocations and name them, but you can't read what the skill returned, and you can't tell from the hook whether it ran inline or forked into a subagent. If you need a skill's verdict, a hook is the wrong instrument.


**Both obvious ways to measure skill usage are wrong, in opposite directions.** Transcript scraping picks up commands that aren’t skills at all. A PreToolUse hook on Skill is blind to every skill a human typed. Each one is missing the half the other one sees, and the two hooks above cover both halves.


Which is a decent illustration of why I bothered writing any of this down. On our side, the blind spot had been filed as a missing platform feature, an ask for Anthropic to *add* a hook on the assumption that plugins had no way to see the typed path. That premise was wrong. The hook already ships, and it’s documented. The fix is a few lines of hook config. The team that filed the ask has shipped it, and our own skill-usage counter is still catching up.


Two things to get right. PostToolUse fires on success, and failures go to the separate PostToolUseFailure event, so count attempts with PreToolUse instead if that's what you want. And the nested case is only half answered, per the two-entry-points section.


Ranked:


1. The two hooks above. Complete, disjoint, documented, real skill names, and it lives entirely inside the plugin.
2. skill_activated with OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS flipped fleetwide. Richer attribution and no code, but it needs an infrastructure change.
3. If neither, keep the scraper but tag the two detectors distinctly and dedupe on session plus name plus timestamp. That at least kills the double-count and makes the pollution filterable.


One footnote: this corrects my own earlier research, which concluded that no hook payload carried a clean command identifier. True of UserPromptSubmit, false of UserPromptExpansion.


### 8. The Same Hook Is a Policy Lever


UserPromptExpansion honors {"decision":"block"}, and it blocks the command *before* any model call happens.


I leaned on this during the research itself. The whole verification matrix ran with expansion blocked, which is how the hook-firing behavior got observed without any of those prompts reaching the model.


For a platform team this is arguably bigger than the counting fix. You can deny specific slash commands org-wide, matched on a clean identifier rather than a text pattern, and the denial costs nothing because it lands before the API call.


Better still, you don’t have to write matching logic. The event’s matcher filters on command name directly, so the config is just the name of the thing you want to stop:


```text
"UserPromptExpansion": [    { "matcher": "some-command", "hooks": [ ... ] }  ]
```


Still reach for a supported setting first where one exists. disableSkillShellExecution kills the shell substitution fleetwide, and the disable-model-invocation and user-invocable frontmatter keys fence a skill to one entry point. The hook is for what those don't cover, which is denying a *specific named* command.


A blocked command ends the run at zero turns, zero API time, and $0. UserPromptSubmit still fires, ahead of the expansion hook, but nothing reaches the model.


The gap is local commands, which UserPromptExpansion never sees. A mod's command.run covers that: it fires for every typed command, and a mod that answers it without calling through stops the command from running. Mods are on by default as of v2.1.287 in the terminal, so if you're the one deploying managed settings, read Anthropic's page on[managing mods for your organization](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/admin) . It covers running your org's own mods ahead of everyone else's, and an allowManagedModsOnly switch that keeps users' mods from loading at all.


### 9. How to Check Any of This Yourself


Three things, all public.


Load any mod with claude --plugin-dir path/to/mod in an interactive session, and Claude Code[writes the TypeScript declarations](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/create) for your exact version into that mod's .claude-plugin/types/: every hook payload, every tool's input and output schema, every mods event.


Write a logging hook. A classic hook that appends its stdin to a file, registered on UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, and PostToolUse, tells you what fires for what. Block on UserPromptExpansion and nothing reaches the model while you poke at it.


Read your own transcripts. They’re JSONL under ~/.claude/projects/, and they're the record of what actually happened, as opposed to what any doc says should happen. I use cq, a tool I wrote that puts SQL on top of them, but jq gets you most of the way.


And stamp the version on everything. Claude Code updates itself often enough that “current” is never a useful stamp. The docs move fast too, in a good way: the public hooks page more than tripled its event list while I was working on this, and the mods docs didn’t exist when I started.


#### Before You Cite This


I tested the hook behavior here against Claude Code v2.1.316 and checked the public docs on the same day. The skill-usage numbers in the counting section come from my own logs on an earlier version. I don’t work on Claude Code, so none of it is guaranteed to stay true. The mechanisms (the four kinds, which hooks see what) should hold up for a while. Anything that’s a list or a count won’t, so quote those with a version attached or not at all.
